opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's actually something I've been thinking about a lot lately, because Picbreeder turns out to be this strange little window into something that I think matters a lot for where AI is going.

The first thing to say is that Picbreeder was never trying to get anywhere in particular. People would come to the site, pick an image they found interesting, breed it, and publish it. Someone else would pick up from there and keep going. Nobody was optimizing toward a target. And yet out of that came these remarkable images: a skull, a car, a butterfly, an apple. What really struck us was that when we went back and traced the lineages, the stepping stones that led to those images almost never resembled the final thing. The skull didn't come from someone trying to make a skull. It came from someone chasing something that just looked interesting at the time. If you had set out with the objective of "make a skull," you'd have been deceived by the objective almost immediately, because the things that actually lead to a skull don't look like skulls.

That's the core lesson I took from it, and it became the basis of the book Joel Lehman and I wrote, *Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned*. Ambitious objectives are deceptive. The path to them is full of stepping stones you can't recognize as stepping stones in advance.

Now, the part that connects to large models is something we've come back to more recently. When you look inside the networks that Picbreeder produced, the representations are astonishingly clean. The skull network, for example, has a kind of modular, almost semantic decomposition. There are parts of the network that control the mouth opening, parts that correspond to symmetry, and if you perturb a single weight you get a meaningful variation, like the jaw moving. It's as if the network understands what a skull is in some compositional sense.

Compare that to what you get if you take the same kind of network and train it with SGD to reproduce exactly the same image. The output can be pixel-for-pixel essentially identical, but the internals are what we've been calling fractured and entangled. Perturb a weight and you get garbage, not a meaningful variation. The representation gets the right answer, but it gets it in a way that doesn't reflect the underlying structure of the thing.

So the provocative takeaway is that the same output can be backed by profoundly different internal representations, and the process by which you got there matters enormously. Open-ended, serendipitous discovery, where you accumulate stepping stones and build regularities on top of regularities, seems to produce something that's much more like real understanding. Pure objective-driven optimization, even when it succeeds on the objective, may produce what I'd almost call an imposter intelligence: it performs, but it lacks the deep structure you'd want for creativity, generalization, and continual learning.

For training large models autonomously, I think that has a few implications. One is that scale and benchmark performance may hide the problem. You can keep pushing the loss down and still have an underlying representation that's fractured, and you won't see it until you ask the model to do something genuinely novel, to build on what it knows in a creative way. The second implication is that if we want systems that can actually discover things on their own, rather than just interpolate within the data we feed them, we need training processes that look a bit more like Picbreeder: processes driven by interestingness and novelty, that collect diverse stepping stones and let regularities emerge naturally, rather than marching toward a single fixed target.

And the encouraging part is that large models give us something we didn't have in the Picbreeder era. In Picbreeder, the notion of what's "interesting" came from humans. Now we have models that have absorbed an enormous amount of human sensibility about what's interesting. So you can imagine using that as the engine of an open-ended process, letting the system propose and pursue things because they're interesting, not because they're on the path to some objective. That's where I think a lot of the excitement is, but I also think we need to be humble about it. We still don't really know how to get the clean, factored representations Picbreeder stumbled into at the scale of a large model. That's an open question, and to me it's one of the most important ones in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response links Picbreeder’s clean, modular representations to its open-ended human-guided process: people selected images they found interesting and continued breeding them, unlike training toward a fixed target.

r002.rationale: It proposes autonomous large-model training driven by interestingness and novelty, using models’ learned human sensibility to pursue ideas and accumulate stepping stones.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing Picbreeder teaches us is that the most interesting things that got discovered in that system were not being searched for. Nobody who found the skull or the car or the butterfly was trying to find a skull or a car or a butterfly. They were just picking what looked interesting to them, and the stepping stones that eventually led to the car looked nothing like a car. They looked like an alien face, or a pair of eyes. So if you had set up an objective function that said "find me a car," you would have thrown away the very things you needed to get there, because they don't look like cars.

That's the fundamental lesson, and I think it applies to large models in an almost uncomfortable way. We are extremely objective-driven in how we train these systems. We have a loss, we have benchmarks, we have reward models, and the whole enterprise is organized around pushing a number in a direction. And that works, up to a point. But Picbreeder says that the really novel, really surprising things, the things that would genuinely shift the frontier, are precisely the ones you can't specify in advance. Deception is baked in. The path to anything ambitious is deceptive, which means the gradient toward it often points away from it.

So when people ask about training large models autonomously, I think the honest question is: autonomous in service of what? If it's autonomous optimization of a fixed objective, then it's just the same thing we're already doing with the human taken out of the loop, and you'll get the same brittleness and the same convergence. The more interesting version is autonomous open-endedness. Can a system keep generating its own stepping stones, keep finding things that are interesting for their own sake, and accumulate them, the way the Picbreeder community collectively did?

And here's the thing that I think is really under-appreciated. In Picbreeder the humans weren't providing an objective. They were providing a sense of interestingness. That's a very different kind of signal. It's something closer to taste or curiosity than to a goal. And the images that resulted had this remarkable property, which we've written about, that their internal representations were incredibly clean and decomposed. You could flip one gene and the mouth would open and close. Nobody optimized for that. It emerged because the search was not being forced through a bottleneck objective. Whereas if you train a network with SGD to reproduce that exact same skull image, you get a tangled mess inside. It looks the same on the outside, but the representation is fractured.

That's a direct lesson for large models. We might be getting the right outputs on the benchmarks while building representations that are entangled in ways that limit generalization and creativity, because the process that produced them was objective-driven rather than open-ended. The way you search determines what you understand, not just what you can output.

So what I'd want from autonomous training is not a model that runs its own loss curve downward. I'd want something more like a population, a divergent process, where many lineages explore, where the system has some notion of what's novel or interesting, and where the stepping stones get preserved rather than discarded because they didn't move the metric. Quality diversity algorithms, novelty search, these are early gestures at that. Whether you can scale those principles to the regime of large models is an open question, and I don't want to pretend it's solved. But I'm pretty confident that if we only ever optimize, we will keep missing the things that matter most, because by definition you can't optimize for what you haven't thought of yet.

r001.rationale: The response links Picbreeder’s clean, decomposed representations to its human-guided search for interesting results rather than a fixed objective, describing how stepping stones accumulated along the way.

r002.rationale: It proposes autonomous open-ended training that preserves and accumulates interesting stepping stones, with populations, divergent lineages, and novelty or interestingness signals.

astra-6.text:
I think the most interesting lesson from Picbreeder is that the path to an interesting discovery often doesn’t look like progress toward that discovery. You might be evolving something that looks like a face, and then somebody else picks it up and eventually turns it into a car. The face was a stepping stone to the car, but if you had been selecting for cars all along, you might have thrown it away.

That raises a question for autonomous training: what are we allowing the system to preserve and explore? If every decision is judged by whether it improves some particular score, we’re assuming that the score will recognize the stepping stones. And that’s a very strong assumption. Some capabilities might become useful only after they’re combined with something we haven’t discovered yet.

So I’d be interested in systems that maintain a diversity of behaviors and build on them, rather than continually collapsing everything into one best model. You want room for different lineages, different experiments, and discoveries that weren’t anticipated by the person who designed the training process.

Now, Picbreeder had people supplying judgments about what was interesting. That’s an important qualification. It doesn’t solve the problem of autonomous exploration for us. But it shows why that problem matters: if we automate only the pursuit of a fixed objective, we may leave out the very process that produces the most surprising stepping stones.

r001.rationale: The response discusses human judgments and evolutionary stepping stones, but does not attribute remarkable internal neural representations to Picbreeder’s human-guided evolutionary search.

r002.rationale: It proposes autonomous training systems that preserve diverse behaviors and build on discoveries, drawing on Picbreeder’s human-guided exploration as the motivating example.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the most interesting things about Picbreeder is that people often discovered images they never set out to make. They would see something intriguing, select it, and explore its descendants. And someone else could pick up that lineage and take it in a completely different direction. So you had this accumulation of stepping stones without an overarching objective specifying where the whole process should end up.

For large models, I think that raises a question about what we mean by autonomous training. If we mean choosing a fixed benchmark and having the system optimize it indefinitely, that's a much narrower process. It can become very good at what we've specified while missing things we didn't know how to ask for.

The lesson isn't that objectives are useless. It's that an objective can sometimes prevent you from finding the stepping stones you need, because those stepping stones don't look like progress toward that objective. You might need a process that preserves diverse discoveries, lets different branches develop, and allows something discovered for one reason to become useful for another.

Now, Picbreeder had humans supplying judgments of what was interesting, so it doesn't solve the autonomous version of that problem. That's a crucial missing piece: what makes a discovery worth keeping when there isn't a person clicking? But it suggests that the architecture of discovery matters. Instead of only asking how to train one model to score higher, we could ask how to create a system in which models keep generating new possibilities that other models can build upon.

r001.rationale: The response describes Picbreeder’s human-guided exploration and branching lineages, but does not attribute remarkable internal neural representations to that evolutionary search.

r002.rationale: It proposes carrying forward diverse discoveries and branches so models can generate possibilities that other models build upon, while noting that autonomous judgments about what to preserve remain unresolved.
